results.title: AWS Raises GPU Prices 15% as Cloud Backlog Hits $2.48T | TechSignal.news
highlights:
TechSignal.news AI November 6, 2026 4 min read

## AWS reprices GPU capacity for the third time in 2026

AWS raised prices for EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML by approximately 15% on October 7 for most U.S. GPU configurations. The increase follows a 15% rise on January 4, a 10% increase in April for selected configurations, and a 20% jump on July 1. Reserved GPU capacity—once positioned as a hedge against spot-market volatility—now exhibits its own price instability.

The repricing reflects demand conditions AWS cannot suppress through incremental capacity additions. Microsoft, Oracle, Amazon and Alphabet disclosed combined cloud backlogs of approximately $2.48 trillion in their latest results: Microsoft $677 billion, Oracle $664 billion, Amazon $578 billion, and Google $561 billion. These commitments represent contracted future revenue, not available infrastructure. For enterprise buyers, the gap between committed spend and deployable capacity creates procurement risk.

AWS competes with Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and specialized GPU providers including CoreWeave and Nebius. Repeated GPU repricing gives rivals an opening to compete on committed-use discounts, reserved capacity and alternative accelerators. Enterprises budgeting for model training or inference should treat GPU capacity as a volatile operating cost rather than a fixed-price reservation. Procurement teams need multi-cloud capacity agreements, longer-term reservations with explicit price-protection clauses, workload portability and documented exposure limits for GPU price changes.

# AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks price increase 2026: p5.48xlarge goes from $31.464 to $47.757 an hour

One email a month with the price changes we confirm on the 355 pricing pages we read. We do not track AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks yet. No card.

AWS raised the price of EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML four times in 2026. In US East (Ohio), p5.48xlarge went from $31.464 to $47.757 an hour per instance. p6-b200.48xlarge went from $74.88 to $113.666. p4d.24xlarge went from $11.8 to $13.57 in October. trn1.32xlarge stayed at $9.532. We do not track AWS on SaaS Price Watch yet. These rates come from the AWS pricing page and archived copies of it. See the AWS public IPv4 price change.

## Old and new prices

Hourly rate per instance in US East (Ohio), in US dollars, as AWS lists them on each date.

Per accelerator, the page now lists p5.48xlarge at $5.970 an hour, up from $3.933 on December 24, 2025. p6-b200.48xlarge is at $14.208, up from $9.36.

Our math: from December 24, 2025 to now, p5.48xlarge is up $16.293 an hour (52%), p5e.48xlarge $20.316 (59%), p5en.48xlarge $26.974 (75%), and p6-b200.48xlarge $38.786 (52%). p4d.24xlarge is up $1.77 (15%). Each step was 10%, 15%, or 20% on the instances that changed. A 24 hour block of one p5.48xlarge now costs $1,146.17, up from $755.14. A one week block of 168 hours costs $8,023.18, up from $5,285.95.

...

## What AWS said

The pricing page says "Reservation prices are updated regularly based on trends in supply and demand for EC2 Capacity Blocks." It now says "The current prices are scheduled to be updated next in January, 2027." The page says "The reservation fee is charged up front at the time you schedule the reservation." It adds "Your Capacity Block is charged at the prevailing rate at the time of purchase, even if the Capacity Block is scheduled to start after the price is updated."

## Who it hits and when

Anyone who books a new Capacity Block pays the rate on the page at purchase. A block bought before an update keeps the rate it was bought at, by the AWS wording above. By the archived copies, the updates landed between December 24, 2025 and January 3, 2026, between March 31 and April 15, 2026, between July 4 and August 25, 2026, and between October 1 and October 10, 2026. The next scheduled update is in January, 2027.

## What to do before your next booking

1. Check the rate for your instance and region on the AWS page before you book.
2. If you plan GPU work for early 2027, book before the January, 2027 update. The new rate could go up or down.
3. Compare p5.48xlarge and p5e.48xlarge per accelerator. The gap changed with each update.
4. Compare On-Demand and Savings Plans prices for long runs.

## What we withhold

We publish US East (Ohio) rates. Other regions list their own rates, and some match. We do not publish p6-b300, UltraServer, or Trainium2 history, because we did not compare them across every update. We do not publish the exact day of each update. We give the window between archived copies.

## FAQ

Did AWS raise Capacity Blocks prices in 2026? Yes. In US East (Ohio), p5.48xlarge went from $31.464 to $47.757 an hour per instance, and p6-b200.48xlarge from $74.88 to $113.666.

How does AWS schedule Capacity Blocks price updates? The page says prices are updated based on supply and demand. In 2026 the archived pages show updates in January, April, the July to August window, and October.

When is the next Capacity Blocks price update? The AWS page says the current prices are scheduled to be updated next in January, 2027.

Does a booked Capacity Block change price? No. AWS charges the prevailing rate at the time of purchase. A later start date does not change that rate.

Did Trainium prices change? No. trn1.32xlarge stayed at $9.532 an hour in US East (Ohio) across every archived copy we read.

## How we check

We read the AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks pricing page on October 26, 2026. We read archived copies of the same page from December 24, 2025 to October 19, 2026, including January 3, March 31, April 15, July 4, August 25, October 1, and October 10, 2026. Get an alert when a cloud price changes.

Checked 2026-10-26. Prices and policies change. Confirm on the source before you buy.

results.title: AWS Capacity Largely Sold out through 2027, with On-Demand Headroom Reserved - InfoQ
results.author: Steef-Jan Wiggers
highlights:
Amazon CEO Andy Jassy recently said that AWS’s large committed cloud capacity is largely sold out through 2027, with a good chunk of 2028 already allocated, while the company continues to reserve headroom for On Demand, EC2 and Bedrock.

Jassy made the remarks in a video podcast with Andreessen Horowitz co-founder Ben Horowitz and general partner Erik Torenberg, reported by Reuters on October 23. AWS sells capacity assurance through On-Demand Capacity Reservations and Capacity Blocks for ML, where a customer reserves instances in a named Availability Zone, and in the Capacity Blocks case, for a fixed window beginning on a future date. As previously reported on InfoQ, AWS raised Capacity Blocks for ML rates by about 15% uniformly across every region in January, covering P5en, P5e, P5 and P4d GPU instances along with Trn2 and Trn1.

Capacity for 2026 is already gone, Jassy said, and the company could invest well beyond the roughly $220 billion in capital expenditure planned for this year without it being a poor use of capital. On the allocation itself:

> 2027 is largely sold out. We always leave a certain amount for on demand and our inference service bedrock, or EC2, but largely sold out all the big chunks. A good chunk of 2028 is sold out.

results.title: AWS is sold out through 2027, and the on demand pool is what's left - Marc Pope
highlights: The price has gone up twice this year. AWS raised EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML pricing by about 15% in January and about 20% on July 1, per Tech Insider's compilation of the pricing pages. The July change hit the P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en and P4de families. A p5e.48xlarge in Ohio went from $34.61 an hour to $39.80 in January alone. AWS called it a "periodic pricing update based on supply and demand," and the pricing page schedules the next one for January 2027. Cloud prices used to go in one direction. Reserved GPU capacity now has an annual repricing cycle, and the direction is up.

results.author: Paul Nugent
highlights:
AWS is raising GPU instance prices by ~20% on July 1 — and quietly keeping its own Trainium chips at the same price.

...

The move: ~20% price increase on EC2 Capacity Block reservations for Nvidia GPU instances, effective July 1. AWS cited "supply and demand dynamics" — meaning the global compute crunch has gotten severe enough that AWS believes customers will pay more without leaving.

The critical detail: Trainium pricing is unchanged.

AWS now operates two parallel compute economics tracks:

🔹 NVIDIA TRACK: +20% — you absorb Nvidia's pricing power, supply constraints, AND AWS's margin protection layered on top.

🔹 TRAINIUM TRACK: flat — Amazon subsidizes the economics because every workload that migrates to Trainium deepens lock-in to the AWS ecosystem.

results.author: Yves Mulkers
highlights:
Andy Jassy, on what is left of the committed capacity at AWS:

“2027 is largely sold out. A good chunk of 2028 is sold out.”

2026 is gone. A slice is held back for on demand, EC2 and Bedrock. Behind the remark sits around $220 billion of capital spending planned for the year, and a quieter move from January, when the price of Capacity Blocks for ML went up about 15% across regions, covering the P5 family, P4d, Trn2 and Trn1.

One person went and looked. The cloud analyst David Linthicum read the same remarks and said he suspects he can still open the AWS console today and allocate GPU capacity for AI work. Both can be true: the big committed blocks are taken, and the tap you actually use still runs.

On EC2, AWS says billing runs in one-second increments with a 60-second minimum, and the purchase menu is wide. Per AWS’s pricing page, Savings Plans advertise savings up to 72% against On-Demand in exchange for a usage commitment, and Spot advertises discounts up to 90% but can be interrupted on two minutes’ notice. For a refresher on the trade-offs, see this EC2 pricing guide covering On-Demand, Spot and Reserved options.

A November 1 report says AWS raised Capacity Blocks for ML rates by about 15% in January 2026, but that is not an official price sheet. Price the commitment against your own downside if a launch slips for lack of GPUs.

results.title: AWS launches support for amortization of EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML - AWS
results.author: Amazon Web Services
highlights:
# AWS launches support for amortization of EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML

 Posted on: Nov 6, 2026 

AWS Data Exports for Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0 and AWS Cost Explorer now amortize the upfront fee for Amazon EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML across the duration of each reservation. You can see the amortized cost of each instance launched into a Capacity Block and the amortized cost of unused capacity, so you can attribute your upfront fee to the workloads that used it and identify capacity that went unused.

Previously, a Capacity Block's upfront fee appeared as a single charge on the purchase date, making it difficult to see how that cost was spread across usage over the reservation. Now the amortized cost appears alongside your instance usage, so you can allocate GPU costs to the teams, projects, and applications that ran on the reserved capacity. You can also see what share of your reservation went unused and plan future Capacity Block purchases. In CUR 2.0, the amortized costs appear in the reservation_amortized_upfront_fee_for_billing_period, reservation_effective_cost columns, and reservation_net_effective_cost shows the amortized cost after discounts. In Cost Explorer, select the amortized cost view to see Capacity Block costs allocated for the reservation.

 Amortization for Capacity Blocks is available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions. To learn more, see the CUR 2.0 data dictionary and exploring your data using Cost Explorer.

A price-list change (Glue 6.0, S3 Vectors, the GPU management fees, Network Firewall, a Bedrock model price) keeps the usage types and lowers the rate. The check is therefore the rate per usage type on either side of the effective date: `line_item_unblended_rate` grouped by `line_item_usage_type` in CUR 2.0, `ListUnitPrice` and `ContractedUnitPrice` in the FOCUS export. A reduction that starts mid-month shows as two rates for one usage type in one month. Nothing has to be done, unless the reduction applies only to a new version, as with Glue 6.0: then the job has to move first, and it pays the old rate until it does. A promotional price with an end date, as for GPT-5.6 Sol, returns to the list price after that day unless AWS extends it. Where the columns sit is in the AWS Cost and Usage Report and FOCUS columns.

results.author: Affiliation: Department of Methodology, StatisticsUtrecht University, The Netherlands
highlights: We convert BYOD time to a rental-equivalent cost using the September 2026 AWS US-East on-demand price of $3.36 per hour for a one-GPU g7e.2xlarge, obtained from the AWS Price List. AWS specifies that this instance contains the same 96-GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU used in our Colab run (Amazon Web Services, 2026c; Amazon Web Services, 2026b). For other systems we use one consistent current major-cloud proxy: $5.191 per accelerator-hour for an AWS p5.4xlarge H100 Capacity Block in US East (Amazon Web Services, 2026a). Thus these figures answer “what would the stated or estimated accelerator-hours cost at a public contemporary rate?”, not what the original authors paid. They exclude storage, egress, idle reservation time, taxes, and discounts.

properties.title: BYOD: Build Your Own DLM - Efficient Autoregressive-to-Diffusion Language Model Conversion
properties.abstract: Unlike autoregressive (AR) models, diffusion language models (DLMs) permit parallel token updates, flexible generation, and bidirectional attention, but leading systems rely on costly pretraining or full-model fine-tuning. We present Build Your Own DLM (BYOD), a generalizable LoRA-only recipe for parameter-efficient AR-to-DLM conversion. Without architecture-specific tuning, BYOD induces diffusion generation in Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Ministral 8B; to our knowledge, this is the first reported AR-to-DLM conversion of a Mistral model. The adapters comprise 4.1-5.8% of final parameters while every base-model parameter remains frozen; each 25,000-iteration conversion needs at most 102.4M tokens, processed in 3.1-4.0 hours on one Google Colab GPU. All four models generate from fully masked sequences, use bidirectional context in a controlled attention test, and retain substantial parent-model knowledge. BYOD-Gemma is the strongest BYOD conversion on our nine-task evaluation, reaching 50.6% average accuracy compared with 51.9% for LLaDA 8B Instruct in the same harness. Open-generation quality at low network function evaluation (NFE) budgets remains the principal limitation: BYOD perplexity is 8.3-11.1 versus 4.1 for LLaDA and 2.2-3.0 for the AR parents when generating 128 tokens in 64 steps. To enable further experimentation and inspection, we provide a standalone training and evaluation implementation and interactive demos for all four conversions. BYOD thus provides a practical route for extending diffusion generation to other existing model families while identifying the gap that efficient conversion must next close.
